title: Drinking While Camping: Cold Nights, Safety and Hangover Tips
excerpt: How to enjoy a few drinks at camp without the misery: why alcohol makes cold nights riskier, water and campfire safety, sleeping in a tent, and how to handle a camping hangover.
metaDescription: Drinking while camping: why alcohol makes cold nights riskier, how to stay hydrated, campfire and swimming safety, and how to beat a camping hangover.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a few drinks around the campfire is a classic part of camping, and for most adults it's fine. What makes camping different from drinking at home is the setting. You're sleeping outside in temperatures you can't control, you're often far from help, the water supply is limited, there's an open fire a few feet away, and the next morning usually involves hiking, packing up, or driving out on a dirt road. Alcohol makes each of those a little harder. A camping hangover also tends to feel worse than a normal one, because you slept on the ground, probably didn't drink enough water, and can't just stay in bed with the blinds closed.

**The quick rules:** Drink more water than you think you need, starting before the first beer. Eat a real dinner before the drinks start. Keep drinks modest on cold nights, because alcohol makes you feel warm while your body actually loses heat faster. Put on your warm layers and get into your sleeping bag before you get drowsy. Keep the fire small and fully put it out before bed. Never swim, climb, or wander off alone after drinking. Make sure the person driving out the next morning is truly sober, which can mean waiting longer than you'd expect after a late night.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide covers general safety and hangover information for social drinkers. **Get help right away (call 911, or use a satellite messenger or emergency beacon if you have no signal) if** someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while very drowsy, is confused or slurring long after they stopped drinking, has blue or pale lips or skin, or is shivering hard, then stops shivering and becomes clumsy or confused. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning or hypothermia, and both are emergencies. Don't let someone "sleep it off" alone in a tent if you're worried. If you're on medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist about drinking, especially if the trip involves heat, cold, or hard exercise.

## Why Drinking While Camping Hits Differently

Alcohol has the same effects on your body whether you're on your couch or at a campsite. The difference is that camping removes most of the cushions that normally soften those effects.

- **You're more dehydrated to start with.** A day of hiking, paddling, setting up camp, or sitting in the sun uses up water. Many people also drink less water while camping because it has to be carried, filtered, or rationed. Alcohol then makes you lose more fluid by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. For more on that, see our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).
- **The temperature swings.** Days can be hot and nights can drop sharply, especially in the mountains and the desert. Alcohol interferes with how your body manages temperature in both directions.
- **Sleep is worse.** Alcohol already breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Add a thin pad, a cold tent, a full bladder, and early sunrise, and many people wake up feeling far worse than the number of drinks would suggest.
- **Help is far away.** Cell service is often spotty, the nearest hospital can be an hour or more away, and paths are dark and uneven. A small mistake, like a stumble near the fire or a wrong turn on the way to the toilet, is harder to recover from.
- **Fatigue stacks up.** Physical effort, sun, wind, and fresh air all make you tired. Many campers notice that the same number of drinks feels stronger after a long day outdoors, mostly because fatigue and dehydration add to alcohol's own effects.

None of this means you can't enjoy a drink. It means the habits that work at a backyard barbecue need a few adjustments in the woods.

## Alcohol, Cold Nights, and Hypothermia

This is the most important safety point in this guide, and it surprises a lot of people.

Alcohol makes you *feel* warmer, but it makes you *lose* heat faster. It widens the small blood vessels near your skin (vasodilation), which sends warm blood toward the surface. That's the flushed, cozy feeling you get by the fire. But that warm blood then gives its heat away to the cold air, and your core temperature can drop. Alcohol also dulls the shivering response, which is one of your body's main ways of making heat, and it blurs your judgment about when you're actually getting cold. We explain the full mechanism in [why alcohol makes you feel warm](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-feel-warm).

Put that together and you have a real risk on cold nights: someone drinks by the fire, feels warm, doesn't put on a jacket, wanders to the tent late, falls asleep in a sleeping bag that isn't zipped or isn't rated for the temperature, and gets dangerously cold without noticing. Hypothermia doesn't need freezing weather. It can happen in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit (roughly 4 to 15°C), especially if someone is wet from rain, sweat, or a swim.

### How to stay warm if you're drinking

- **Layer up before you feel cold.** Put on your warm layers, hat, and dry socks when the sun goes down, not when you start shivering.
- **Get dry.** Change out of sweaty or damp clothes before the evening starts. Wet clothing pulls heat away from your body much faster than dry clothing does.
- **Keep the drinks modest on cold nights.** The colder the forecast, the more conservative you should be.
- **Eat a warm, filling dinner.** Your body burns food to make heat overnight. A high-calorie meal before bed helps.
- **Go to bed before you're sleepy-drunk.** Set up your sleeping bag and pad early, while you're still clear-headed, so you're not fumbling with zippers in the dark.
- **Use the buddy system.** Check on friends who were drinking before you go to sleep. Make sure they're actually in their bag and dressed for the night.

### Warning signs of hypothermia

Early hypothermia looks a lot like being drunk: shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, poor judgment, and confusion. That overlap is exactly what makes it dangerous, because friends may assume someone is "just drunk." Watch for these signs, especially in someone who's been drinking on a cold night:

- Heavy shivering that won't stop, or shivering that *stops* while the person still seems cold and confused
- Stumbling, fumbling hands, or slurred speech that gets worse instead of better
- Drowsiness, very low energy, or acting strangely
- Cold, pale skin

If you suspect hypothermia, get the person out of the wind and wet, replace wet clothes with dry ones, wrap them in sleeping bags or blankets (a warm body next to them in the bag helps), and give warm, sweet, non-alcoholic drinks if they're awake and can swallow normally. Don't give more alcohol to "warm them up." If they're confused, very drowsy, or not improving, treat it as an emergency and get help.

## Alcohol in Hot Weather and Desert Camping

Summer and desert camping bring the opposite problem. In heat, your body cools itself by sweating, which uses a lot of water. Alcohol adds to the fluid loss and can make it harder to notice that you're overheating.

Day drinking in the sun is where most heat problems start. A few beers on a sunny lake shore or a hot trail can turn into dehydration, a pounding headache, and in the worst cases heat exhaustion. Signs of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, headache, weakness, and a fast pulse. Move to shade, drink water, cool the skin with wet cloth, and rest. Confusion, fainting, or hot skin that has stopped sweating can mean heatstroke, which is a medical emergency.

Practical tips for warm-weather trips:

- Save the drinks for the evening, after the hottest part of the day.
- Keep a water bottle in hand alongside every alcoholic drink.
- Stay in shade and wear a hat.
- Add electrolytes to some of your water, especially after sweating a lot. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains when they help and when plain water is enough.

Our [day drinking guide](/never-hungover/day-drinking) covers pacing in the sun in more detail.

## Water: The Single Biggest Camping Hangover Factor

If there's one thing that separates a rough camping morning from a fine one, it's water. Most camping hangovers are made noticeably worse by simple dehydration.

At home you can drink a big glass of water before bed without thinking about it. At camp, water might be in a jug you have to refill, a lake you have to filter, or a pump you have to walk to. People ration it without realizing, then drink beer instead because it's cold and right there.

**How to plan for it:**

- **Bring or plan more water than you think you need.** Count drinking water, cooking water, and water for the morning after. If you're relying on a filter, filter a full supply before dark so you're not doing it tipsy with a headlamp.
- **Use a simple rule: one water for every drink.** Keep a full bottle next to your camp chair and finish it as you go.
- **Put a full bottle in the tent.** You'll want it at 3 a.m. and again at sunrise.
- **Never drink untreated water because you're thirsty and impaired.** Streams and lakes can carry parasites and bacteria that cause days of stomach problems. Treat or filter it, every time.
- **Pack an electrolyte mix.** It doesn't take up much space and can help when you've been sweating all day and drinking all night.

Water won't stop a hangover on its own, since hangovers also involve inflammation, poor sleep, and by-products of alcohol breakdown. But dehydration makes headaches, dizziness, and fatigue worse, and it's the easiest part to fix.

## Campfire and Stove Safety After Drinking

Fire is part of the fun, and it's also where drinking at camp most often goes wrong. Alcohol slows reaction time, makes you misjudge distances, and loosens caution, all of which matter when you're standing next to open flames.

- **Keep the fire a reasonable size.** Big fires are harder to control, especially in wind. Follow any fire restrictions or burn bans for the area, which can change daily in dry seasons.
- **Set the seating back from the fire.** Leave a clear zone around the fire ring so nobody trips into it.
- **Never use gasoline, lighter fluid, or alcohol to boost a fire.** Flare-ups are a common cause of serious burns.
- **Watch the high-proof drinks near the flames.** Spirits are flammable. Don't pour them near the fire or try fire tricks.
- **Assign someone sober-ish to put the fire out.** Drown it with water, stir the ashes, and drown it again until it's cold to the touch. Don't leave a fire burning while everyone falls asleep.
- **Never bring a stove, grill, charcoal, or fuel-burning heater into a tent.** They produce carbon monoxide, an odorless gas that can kill people while they sleep, and alcohol makes it harder to notice early symptoms like headache and dizziness. Use only heaters specifically designed and rated for indoor tent use, and follow the manufacturer's instructions exactly.

## Swimming, Hiking, and Wandering Off

Water and dark trails are the two other big risks after drinking at camp.

**Swimming.** Alcohol affects coordination, judgment of distance and currents, and your ability to handle cold water. Lakes and rivers can be much colder than they look, and cold water causes a gasp reflex that can lead to inhaling water. If you've been drinking, stay out of the water, especially at night. If you're going to paddle or swim the next morning, make sure you've had enough time to recover, wear a life jacket, and never go alone. Many of the same points are covered in our guide on [drinking on a boat](/never-hungover/drinking-on-a-boat).

**Night walks.** Trips to the toilet or a friend's site after dark are where many falls and sprained ankles happen. Use a headlamp, take the same path you know, and bring a friend if you're unsteady. Don't go off-trail to "look at the stars" alone.

**Climbing and scrambling.** Leave rocks, cliffs, and steep banks alone after drinking. Every year people are hurt in falls that started with a casual climb after a few beers.

**The next day's hike.** Hiking hungover is uncomfortable but usually doable on an easy trail. On a hard, hot, or high trail, it's a real risk, because you're starting dehydrated, under-slept, and less coordinated. Choose a shorter route, start later after you've eaten and rehydrated, and turn back if you feel dizzy or very weak.

## Camping at Altitude

Many favorite campsites are in the mountains, and altitude adds another layer. At higher elevations you lose more water through breathing, and many people sleep worse even without alcohol. Some people also feel alcohol more strongly when they're not used to the altitude, partly because the symptoms of early altitude sickness (headache, nausea, fatigue, poor sleep) overlap so much with a hangover that they're hard to tell apart.

If you've just arrived at a high campsite, it's wise to go easy the first night, drink plenty of water, and see how you feel. If a "hangover" headache gets worse instead of better, or comes with breathlessness at rest, confusion, or trouble walking, descend and get help, because those can be signs of serious altitude illness. Our [altitude and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/altitude-alcohol-high-elevation-drinking-safety-2025) goes into more detail.

## Rules, Wildlife, and Leave No Trace

Before you pack the cooler, check the rules where you're going. Alcohol rules vary widely between national parks, national forests, state parks, county parks, and private campgrounds. Some allow alcohol at your site but not on beaches or trails, some ban it during holiday weekends, some ban glass containers, and some don't allow it at all. Campground hosts and rangers can enforce these rules with fines or by asking you to leave. Open-container laws still apply in your vehicle.

A few other things to keep in mind:

- **Store alcohol like food in bear country.** Bears and other animals are attracted to the smell of sugary drinks, beer cans, and coolers. Put drinks, empties, and trash in a bear box, bear canister, or locked hard-sided vehicle as the area requires, and never keep them in your tent.
- **Pack cans instead of glass.** Cans are lighter, easier to pack out, and don't leave broken glass that can cut bare feet or wildlife.
- **Pack out everything.** Bottle caps, cans, and wrappers are some of the most common litter at campsites. Crush cans and bring a bag for empties.
- **Respect quiet hours.** Sound carries far at night outdoors, and drinking tends to make groups louder than they realize.

## Sleeping in a Tent After Drinking

Even a few drinks can make tent sleep rough. Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster but tends to cause lighter, broken sleep later in the night as your body processes it, along with more trips to pee. In a tent, that might mean crawling out into the cold at 2 a.m.

To give yourself a better night:

- Stop drinking a couple of hours before bed if you can.
- Have a last big glass of water about an hour before sleep, then use the toilet right before you get in your bag.
- Keep a pee bottle or a clear path to the toilet, plus a headlamp within reach.
- Use a pad with enough insulation for the night's temperature. A lot of "hangover" misery at camp is really cold, broken sleep from a thin pad.
- Wear a warm hat and dry socks.
- If you tend to wake up nauseated, set yourself up near the door and keep a bag within reach.

Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the science behind alcohol and broken sleep.

## How to Prevent a Camping Hangover

There's no trick that guarantees a hangover-free morning, other than drinking less. But a few habits make a real difference:

1. **Eat a solid dinner before drinking.** Food slows how fast alcohol enters your blood. Campfire classics like burgers, chili, foil-packet potatoes, and pasta are all good choices.
2. **Pace yourself.** Your liver clears alcohol at a roughly fixed rate, often estimated at about one standard drink per hour for an average adult, and nothing speeds it up much. Long evenings around the fire make it easy to drink steadily for six hours without noticing the total.
3. **Count drinks honestly.** Camp pours are often generous, and craft beers can be much stronger than a standard 5% beer.
4. **Alternate with water.** One for one.
5. **Choose lighter options.** Lower-alcohol beers and drinks let you stay social longer with less of a toll. Some people also find that darker spirits give them worse hangovers, possibly because of natural by-products of fermentation called congeners, though individual responses vary.
6. **Skip mixing in drinking games.** Shots and games are the fastest way from a pleasant evening to a terrible morning.
7. **Get to bed warm and hydrated.** Sleep quality matters more for how you feel than most people expect.

For a deeper look at prevention, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## What to Do If You Wake Up Hungover at Camp

So you overdid it. Here's how to get through the morning in the woods.

- **Drink water first, slowly.** Small sips if your stomach is uneasy. Add an electrolyte packet if you have one.
- **Eat something simple.** Oatmeal, toast, bananas, eggs, or crackers are easy on the stomach. A hot breakfast cooked on the stove can help you feel human again. Our list of the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) has more ideas that travel well.
- **Get into shade, or out of the cold.** Temperature extremes make headaches and nausea worse.
- **Take it slow on camp chores.** Pack up carefully, double-check that the fire is completely out, and don't rush.
- **Be careful with pain relievers.** If you take one, stick to the label dose and take it with food and water. Ibuprofen and naproxen can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already upset, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds work for the liver, so avoid taking it while alcohol is still in your system or using more than the label allows.
- **Coffee is fine in moderation,** but it doesn't sober you up and won't replace water.
- **Don't treat the hangover with more alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" just delays the hangover and adds to the alcohol still in your system.

### Driving out the next morning

This one matters. After a long night of drinking, you may still be over the legal limit when you wake up, even if you feel okay. Your body clears alcohol at a fixed pace, and sleep, coffee, and cold showers don't speed it up. Camp exits often mean dirt roads, mountain curves, and tired drivers, which leave little room for error. Plan ahead: the designated driver should drink little or nothing the night before, or the group should wait until midday or later to leave. If you're not sure, don't drive.

## When a Camping Hangover Is Something More

Most hangovers fade within a day. But in the outdoors, the symptoms of a few more serious problems can look a lot like a hangover. Get help, or at least take them seriously, if you notice:

- **Signs of alcohol poisoning** during the night: someone who can't be woken, slow or irregular breathing, vomiting while barely conscious, seizures, or very pale or bluish skin. Put them on their side to prevent choking, stay with them, and call for help. Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains what to look for.
- **Signs of hypothermia** after a cold night, as described above.
- **Signs of heat illness** after a hot day: confusion, fainting, or very high body temperature.
- **Signs of altitude illness** that get worse instead of better.
- **Carbon monoxide symptoms** such as headache, dizziness, and nausea in more than one person who slept near a stove or heater. Get everyone into fresh air immediately.
- **Severe or prolonged vomiting** that keeps you from holding down water for many hours, which can cause dangerous dehydration.
- **Shakes, sweating, anxiety, or racing heart** that come on when you go without alcohol for a while, especially if you drink heavily most days. That can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, and it deserves a conversation with a doctor rather than another drink.

Know your nearest ranger station or emergency route before the trip, and if you're going somewhere with no cell service, consider carrying a satellite messenger or personal locator beacon.

## A Simple Camping Drinks Checklist

Pack these and you'll have most of what you need for a good night and a decent morning:

- More water than you think you need, or a reliable filter and a full supply filtered before dark
- Electrolyte packets
- Cans instead of glass, and a bag for empties
- A real dinner and an easy breakfast
- Warm layers, a hat, and dry socks for the evening
- A sleeping bag and pad rated for the night's low temperature
- A headlamp for everyone
- A fire extinguisher, bucket of water, or shovel for the fire
- Basic pain relievers and anti-nausea items you know you tolerate
- A plan for who drives out, and when

## Where DHM Fits In

Some campers pack a DHM supplement. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research so far is in animals, and human evidence is limited. Some people find that taking it with their drinks or before bed helps them feel better the next morning, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers, and it does nothing to lower your blood alcohol, keep you warm, or make it safe to swim, hike, or drive after drinking. Water, food, warmth, and sensible pacing matter far more.

If you'd like to try it, a popular choice is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and for a lower cost per serving there's [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Both are small enough to pack in a toiletry bag. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it.

## The Bottom Line

Drinking while camping can be a great part of a trip, as long as you respect the setting. Drink water steadily, eat a real dinner, layer up before the cold sets in, keep the fire small and put it out properly, stay out of the water and off the rocks after dark, and give yourself plenty of time before anyone drives out. Those habits make the night safer and the morning a lot easier.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is it safe to drink alcohol while camping?**

For most adults, a few drinks at camp is fine as long as you plan for the setting. Drink plenty of water, eat a real meal, dress warmly before the evening cools down, keep the campfire under control, and stay out of the water and off steep ground after drinking. Check the campground's rules first, since some parks restrict or ban alcohol.

**Does alcohol keep you warm when camping?**

No. Alcohol makes you feel warm by widening blood vessels near your skin, but that sends heat out of your body faster and can lower your core temperature. It also dulls shivering and your sense of how cold you are. On cold nights, keep drinks modest and put on warm layers before you feel chilly.

**Why are camping hangovers so bad?**

Camping stacks several things that make hangovers worse: dehydration from a day outdoors and limited water, poor sleep on the ground, cold or hot temperatures, and long, slow evenings of drinking that add up. Drinking a full bottle of water for every drink and sleeping warm make the biggest difference.

**How do you cure a hangover while camping?**

There's no real cure besides time, but you can feel better faster. Sip water with electrolytes, eat a simple breakfast like oatmeal, eggs, or toast, get into shade or out of the cold, and take it easy. If you use a pain reliever, take the label dose with food. Avoid more alcohol, and don't drive until you're sure the alcohol has cleared.

**Can you drink alcohol in national parks and state parks?**

It depends on the park. Many national parks allow alcohol at campsites but restrict it in certain areas, and some state and county parks ban it entirely or during holiday weekends. Glass containers are often prohibited in some areas. Check the park's website or ask the campground host before you go.

**Can you get hypothermia from drinking outside?**

Yes. Alcohol increases heat loss and dulls the shivering response and your judgment, and hypothermia can happen well above freezing, especially if you're wet or windy. Warning signs include uncontrollable shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, and confusion, which can be mistaken for drunkenness. Get the person warm and dry, and get help if they're confused or not improving.

**Can I drive home from camping the morning after drinking?**

Not always. After a late night of heavy drinking, you can still be over the legal limit the next morning, and sleep or coffee doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol. Have the designated driver drink little or nothing the night before, or wait until later in the day to leave.

**Does DHM help with camping hangovers?**

Some people take DHM with their drinks or before bed and feel it helps the next morning, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers, and most of the research is in animals. It doesn't keep you warm, lower your blood alcohol, or make swimming or driving safe after drinking. Water, food, warmth, and pacing matter more.
